note.note:
Consult Summary:
- Adult patient with 1-week history of sore throat progressing to dry cough, mild exertional shortness of breath, occasional wheeze, intermittent low-grade fever/headache, and reduced appetite; clinician provided reassurance for a presumed viral upper respiratory infection, advised symptomatic care, safety-netting, and issued a sick note.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Sore throat × ~7 days, followed 1–2 days later by dry, non-productive cough.
- Symptom timeline:
  • Day 0 (Thu/Fri last week): Sore throat began.  
  • Day 1–2: Dry cough started.  
  • Day 3–4: Onset of exertional shortness of breath, mild wheeze, and some chest discomfort.  
  • First 3 days: Subjective fever; now resolved.  
  • Intermittent headaches noted; none at time of consult.
- Current status: Symptoms fluctuate (“better then worse”), overall mild and not limiting normal activity; cough same day and night.
- Associated symptoms: Reduced appetite; denies sputum, haemoptysis, nasal/sinus congestion, rashes, or weight loss.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors: SOB only on exertion; no nocturnal worsening; no specific relief measures reported.
- Review of systems (pertinent negatives unless stated): No persistent fever, no significant weight change, no night sweats, no skin rash, no neck lumps, no recent significant travel, no known asbestos exposure.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic medical conditions reported.
- No history of asthma or thromboembolic disease.

Medications:
- None reported.

Allergies:
- Peanut allergy (no drug allergies).

Social History:
- Non-smoker (one-time experimentation only); no regular alcohol or substance use documented.
- Occupation not specified; required 2 sick days (Tue & Thu this week) due to illness.
- Born in the United States; resident in the UK for >12 years; recent travel limited to Europe.

Family History:
- Mother: Lung cancer.
- No family history of clotting disorders.

Physical Examination:
- Remote video consultation; no formal exam performed.
- Patient palpated neck: no lumps or bumps.
- Vitals not recorded.

Investigations:
- None performed or available during this consultation.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Probable acute viral upper respiratory tract infection / viral bronchitis
  - Assessment: Classic sequence and course of viral illness; mild symptoms improving overall; no red-flag features.
  - Plan:
    • Symptomatic treatment: Paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented) for pain/fever.  
    • Encourage adequate oral fluids and rest.  
    • Expect improvement within ~4–5 days; if not improving or worsening, seek in-person medical review.  
    • Reassurance provided regarding low likelihood of tuberculosis or lung cancer at this stage.

Issue 2: Mild exertional dyspnoea with wheeze – consider reactive airway involvement
  - Assessment: Likely transient airway irritation from viral infection; new-onset asthma less likely but possible.
  - Plan:
    • Monitor for persistence or worsening of wheeze/SOB.  
    • Advise urgent GP review or emergency care if breathlessness suddenly increases or occurs at rest.

Issue 3: Occupational impact
  - Plan:
    • Fit note (“sick note”) provided for additional days off work to recuperate.

General safety-netting:
  - Seek immediate care for severe breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, persistent fever, or any other concerning change.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute viral upper respiratory infection / viral bronchitis – High likelihood  
   Reasoning: Typical sore throat → dry cough sequence, low-grade fever, self-limiting course, absence of bacterial signs.
2. COVID-19 infection – Moderate likelihood  
   Reasoning: Symptom constellation (sore throat, dry cough, fever, headache, appetite loss) fits; no test performed, no anosmia reported.
3. Reactive airway disease / new-onset asthma – Moderate likelihood  
   Reasoning: Dry cough, exertional SOB, wheeze; could be virus-triggered first episode; no prior asthma history.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing elements: No vital signs, no physical examination findings besides patient self-inspection; medication doses not documented.  
● Conflicts: Patient both affirmed and later denied chest pain during conversation – conflict noted. Date of birth (09 May 2016) inconsistent with adult history – conflict noted.  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor overlaps and time constraints at end.
